content: People living with HIV and drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) should begin second-line anti-TB drugs as soon as possible, ideally within the first eight weeks of starting anti-TB treatment, regardless of their CD4 cell count. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-certainty evidence, as outlined in the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment for drug-resistant TB. The WHO has recently updated its guidance on drug-resistant TB, including recommendations for regimens targeting rifampicin-susceptible but isoniazid-resistant TB, shorter all-oral regimens containing bedaquiline for multidrugor rifampicin-resistant TB, and longer regimens for these forms of TB. While there is potential for overlapping or additive toxicities and drug-drug interactions between certain antiretroviral (ARV) drugs and injectable agents like moxifloxacin and clofazimine, these interactions generally do not necessitate changes to the regimens for multidrug-resistant TB or antiretroviral therapy (ART). However, the WHO advises against the combined use of bedaquiline and efavirenz. ART regimens should be optimized and initiated early, in line with WHO recommendations. Close monitoring for both treatment response and toxicity is essential for individuals receiving concurrent TB and HIV treatment. Additionally, other comorbidities, such as diabetes and mental health disorders, should be managed appropriately. Evidence from 10 studies was reviewed to assess treatment outcomes when ART and second-line anti-TB drugs were used together. None of the data came from randomized controlled trials, and individual data were available for 217 people with drug-resistant TB, of whom 127 received ART. The certainty of evidence from these observational studies ranged from low to very low. Latent TB is defined as a state of persistent immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without evidence of clinically active TB disease. Approximately one-quarter of the global population is infected with TB. Among people living with HIV, the combined use of TB preventive treatment and ART has demonstrated benefits in reducing both TB incidence and mortality, even in individuals with higher CD4 cell counts. Adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB should receive TB preventive treatment as part of comprehensive HIV care. This includes those on ART, pregnant women, and individuals previously treated for TB, regardless of the degree of immunosuppression or availability of latent TB infection testing. Infants under 12 months of age living with HIV who have been in contact with a person with TB and are unlikely to have active TB should also receive TB preventive treatment following appropriate clinical evaluation. Children aged 12 months or older living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB should be offered TB preventive treatment as part of comprehensive HIV care, especially in settings with high TB transmission. All children living with HIV who have successfully completed treatment for TB disease may also receive TB preventive treatment. Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those without symptoms such as current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have active TB and should be offered preventive treatment, regardless of their ART status. Individuals with any of these symptoms should be evaluated for TB and other diseases, and preventive treatment should be offered if active TB is excluded. Chest radiography may be offered to people living with HIV receiving ART and TB preventive treatment, provided there are no abnormal radiographic findings. Infants and children living with HIV who exhibit poor weight gain, fever, or current cough, or who have been in contact with a person with TB, should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. If active TB is excluded, they should be offered TB preventive treatment regardless of age. Testing for latent TB infection can be done using either a tuberculin skin test or an interferon-gamma release assay. TB preventive treatment options include six or nine months of daily isoniazid, a three-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a three-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. A one-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or four months of daily rifampicin alone may also be offered as alternatives. In high TB transmission settings, adults and adolescents living with HIV who have a positive or unknown latent TB infection test and are unlikely to have active TB should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy. This therapy should be provided regardless of ART status, degree of immunosuppression, history of previous TB treatment, or pregnancy. Pregnancy should not disqualify women living with HIV from receiving TB preventive treatment with medicines like isoniazid and rifampicin, which are generally considered safe during pregnancy. For infants under 12 months of age living with HIV, TB preventive treatment should be given only to those with a history of household contact with a person with TB and no evidence of active TB disease, as per national guidelines. Regimens containing rifamycins should be prescribed cautiously to people living with HIV who are on ART due to potential drug-drug interactions. For example, rifampicin can reduce the concentrations of certain protease inhibitors (PIs) like atazanavir, darunavir, and lopinavir. However, no dose adjustment is needed when rifampicin is co-administered with efavirenz. The dose of dolutegravir (DTG) should be increased to 50 mg twice daily when given with rifampicin, and this dosing should continue for an additional two weeks after stopping rifampicin. The WHO End TB Strategy aims for a 90% reduction in TB deaths and an 80% decrease in TB incidence by 2030. This strategy emphasizes prevention, including infection control in healthcare settings and other high-risk environments.
